storm.summary_layperson: No storms on radar right now. The National Weather Service flags a slight chance of an isolated shower or rumble of thunder before sundown, but nothing organized is tracking toward the cove this evening.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound's protective marine layer is already weak (6°F air–water gap) and fades to almost nothing by 7 PM as the air cools — there's little buffer left for anything that develops later in the window.
storm.detail_html:
The National Weather Service (OKX) is carrying a slight chance of showers and thunderstorms this afternoon and evening, driven by weak capping and modest instability that could support isolated to scattered development until shortly after sundown. As of this run, radar out of KOKX shows a completely clean scope — no cells being tracked toward the cove.

Instability is modest (CAPE 1,180 J/kg, rising only slightly toward 1,370 J/kg by 7 PM) but wind shear is unusually strong for that amount of fuel (34 kt through 0–6 km). That combination means if something does fire, it's more likely to produce a brief strong gust than a heavy rain event — the atmosphere is capped enough to keep storms isolated rather than widespread.

The Sound's usual defense — a cool marine layer that chokes incoming storms — is only weak today. The air–water gap is 6.1°F now (water 74.5°F, air 80.6°F), which is enough to register but not enough to call the layer strong. And that gap is closing fast: as the sun angle drops and air temperature falls through the evening, the gap narrows to 3.9°F by 6 PM and near-zero (1.1°F) by 7 PM. The buffer effectively disappears by around 5:12 PM — right as this wind window opens.

Net call for the 5–10 PM window: most likely a dry evening with at most an isolated sprinkle or distant rumble, and no meaningful edge for the cove over surrounding towns since there's no cell in play to benefit from Sound cooling in the first place. The moderate risk / mitigating-effect scenarios in the framework simply aren't active tonight.

What would change this call: any cell appearing on KOKX radar approaching from the W–NW–SW this evening, or CAPE climbing past 1,500–3,000 J/kg (the punch-through range where the marine layer stops being able to choke a storm). Given the shear/CAPE mismatch, watch particularly for wind-driven damage reports rather than flooding rain if anything does develop.

wind.tactics_blurb: SW–SSW sea breeze reinforced by a light onshore gradient, easing from around 8–10 kt early to 4–6 kt after sunset (7:40 PM). Start mid-line and work the right — the shift is still building today, not yet in a clean oscillation.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today qualifies as a sea-breeze day: the air–water temperature difference (deltaT) is 6.1°F, above the 5°F threshold needed for a thermal circulation, and the background gradient is a light onshore southerly (~7 kt from the airport-network average) rather than calm or offshore. That onshore gradient doesn't fight the sea breeze — it reinforces it, which is why this is a reinforced sea-breeze day rather than a pure thermal one: expect it stronger and steadier than a thermal-only afternoon, and expect it to hold 30–60 minutes past the normal sunset collapse because the gradient flow keeps blowing after the thermal engine shuts off.

The deltaT hasn't reached the 8°F gate this framework uses to call a sea breeze "mature," and it's actually falling through the evening (6.1°F now → 3.9°F by 6 PM → ~1°F by 7 PM) as the air cools faster than the Sound. That means today's breeze likely never fully matures into the clean oscillating pattern — it stays in the persistent, right-shifting phase the whole window. Favor the right on the beat for that reason, plus the cove geography: SW–SSW flow is fairly uniform across the course but runs slightly stronger toward the mouth and east shore (less shelter from Tod's Point on that side).

One flag worth knowing: HRRR's near-term forecast direction (198–220° SSW/SW) is running about 20° backed from what stations are reading right now (218° SW at the western-LIS ensemble). Confidence on direction is moderate — HRRR is known to lag the afternoon veer of this sea breeze, but the correction engine didn't kick in because deltaT hasn't hit its 8°F gate yet. Practical read: actual direction this evening may run a touch more SW than the hourly table shows.

In kt terms: 8–10 kt through 6 PM is comfortable racing for most one-design fleets, easing to 5–7 kt by 8 PM as the thermal fades and the background southerly (not a true sea breeze anymore past that point) does the remaining work, and dropping into drifter range (4–6 kt) by 9–10 PM. Last start of the evening is the one to watch for AP risk.

Data note: HRRR's model output for this run only extends to 7 PM local; the 8–10 PM figures above are extrapolated from this reinforced-sea-breeze framework (gradient persisting after thermal collapse, gradual nocturnal softening) rather than pulled from raw model output — treat the late hours as directional guidance, not a precise forecast.

data_caveats: HRRR wind/temperature model output is only available through 7:00 PM local (f01–f04); the 8:00–10:00 PM wind figures are extrapolated from the reinforced-sea-breeze framework, not raw model output.
RAP CAPE was unavailable this run; instability context was pulled from a single OKX AFD mention as a fallback.
3 METAR stations (KHPN, KISP, KFRG) have anemometer or wind-sensor outages this run and were excluded from the gradient-wind reading.

HRRR's near-term wind direction (198–220° SSW/SW) is running ~20° backed from current station obs (218° SW); the sea breeze hasn't reached the 8°F maturation gate (currently 6.1°F) so the model-lag correction wasn't applied — actual direction may run more SW than shown.
